title: Yiyun Li reveals life lessons in her new symphonic novel
text:
Yiyun Li reveals life lessons in her new symphonic novel
“I said something preposterous to a friend, but I really do stand by it,” Yiyun Li tells me on the other end of a screen in her home in Princeton, New Jersey. “I have written everything I know about life into this novel.”
That claim might seem hard to believe. Li has written 12 other books ranging from novels (both historical and contemporary) to short-story collections, memoirs, and even a picture book. They all carry her signature observational style, laced through with a dry, unflinching wit that’s not afraid to address either the sunny or dark aspects of the human condition.
In person (or rather, over Zoom), Li speaks with a quiet confidence and charm that is disarming in the most positive sense of the word. But it’s her genuine humility that shines through. Li doesn’t seem very interested in discussing her many accomplishments, instead focusing on the craft of writing – which is notable, given that she received a Pulitzer this year for her 2025 memoir “Things in Nature Merely Grow.” The significance of that win, a capstone achievement in any writer’s career, is tempered by the book’s subject matter: how one of her sons took his own life several years after his brother did the same. The memoir is about the persistence of life in the face of death. “The verb that does not die is ‘to be,’” she wrote. “Vincent was and is and will always be Vincent. James was and is and will always be James.”
The esteemed author won a Pulitzer Prize this year. She’d chatted with The Monitor about how writing her latest book was inspired by everything she's learned from life (and piano lessons).
“Music Against the Night” is a very different kind of book. It’s Li’s return to historical fiction. She previously took on the genre in her novel “The Book of Goose,” which concerned two childhood friends who commit a literary hoax in postwar France. Li finished a first draft of the novel before starting her aforementioned memoir, and then revised it afterward. That first draft was initially 200,000 words. Li ended up cutting 100,000 of them – the equivalent of nixing a whole novel. “At the beginning and end of every day, I see how many words I cut,” she says with a small smile. “I always have a number.”
The novel is the first in a trilogy that follows two piano prodigies on course for a romantic collision in the early 1800s. The characters haven’t been invented. The novel is a fictionalized account of two actual historical figures: John Field, an Irish performer and composer who is credited with creating the nocturne (though that honor is often given to Chopin), and his wife, Adelaide Percheron, a pianist nicknamed Percherette from French India. The narrative traces the two of them from childhood into adulthood as they pursue their ambitions across the globe. As they do so, they’re drawn ever-closer together in an inevitable gravity, resulting in a marriage that is as much a standoff as it is a partnership.
Neither John Field nor Percherette have been given very much exposure in the general public’s understanding of music history. Li tells me that most musicians aren’t aware of Field and “only deep pianists will know his name.” She herself came across him in an unexpected place – a footnote in a biography of Leo Tolstoy. (She previously published “Tolstoy Together: 85 Days of War and Peace With Yiyun Li,” an account of her public reading group devoted to the Russian novelist.)
Though Li never says it in so many words, this was the start of a fascination. In a biography of John Field, she was surprised to find that his wife, Percherette, is only mentioned in five paragraphs and a footnote. There’s no other scholarship around Percherette, despite her tremendous talent as a musician.
“I’m always interested in people who become footnotes for other people,” Li says. Field was one footnote, and Percherette, a footnote within a footnote.
“Music Against the Night” is populated with other historical figures, both major and minor, and it gives the novel a distinctive texture. The narrative winds in and out of time, masterfully jumping between past and future with no consideration to chronology. Digression and progression are the necessary path to arrive at the full truth of the characters’ intertwined stories. By her own admission, the preludes and parallels of a musical composition are woven into the very structure of the novel.
“When you write a novel about music,” Li says, “you almost have to rely on musical patterns. First you develop the theme, and then the counterpoint. The form of the novel has to be informed by the form of music as we know it.”
Li engaged in an enormous amount of research. She read primary sources such as a travelogue of an English woman journeying from England to India; accounts of people living in Paris, Dublin, Bath, and St. Petersburg; plus records of migration and the slave trade. But that wasn’t enough to get into the frame of mind of a person from the Romantic era. Li also needed to get into the mindset of a musician. To paraphrase a friend of hers, she went “full method” on this project. Li, who had started learning to play piano following the death of her children, found a music teacher who was an expert in Romantic-era music. She was the piano teacher’s only adult student. The author was only able to enroll in lessons after pitching the idea of her novel to the tutor. Li’s knowledge of John Field was the key that opened that door.
The two characters in the novel are very different personalities despite their continual orbit of each other. Where John begins as a gentle and naive child, driven by a natural-born creativity, Percherette is shrewd and possesses a curiosity driven by the engine of her ambition. And while the novel focuses on these two individuals, there is another character who shares the spotlight – namely the narrator.
The fact of the narrator being a protagonist, in a way, is undeniable. That voice is the reader’s companion and guide, grounding the narrative as it sweeps backward and forward in time. More than that, it acts almost as an oracle, giving out answers when none of the other characters can.
When I mention this, Li gives me another conspiratorial smile. “I actually strongly believe that an omniscient narrator should always be a character,” she says, as if she is imparting a secret, sharing something that she’s incredibly pleased to have gotten away with. The narrator dispenses observations that can be bitter or kind, with a hard-won wisdom. “To be known is the desire that drives much of the world’s progress, also much of its destruction,” says the narrator, handing out this gleaming insight as casually as reporting the weather.
While it would be reductive to say that this narrator is Li, that voice is certainly informed by her experiences. It is the vehicle for all that she’s learned.
The story follows the characters in each stage of their lives. Li’s perspective comes through when the narrator describes a particularly significant period in Percherette’s life.
“A child’s death can never feel natural to a parent,” the narrator says. “A child’s death is a negation of time, which no longer has now and then, now and again, now and later, only now and now and now and now.” “Music Against the Night” demands that we examine our lives as they are, without distortion or sentiment, be that good or ill. And it asks, with a direct and piercing stare: What sustains us when everything else falls away?
“I’ve thought a lot about losses and deaths. About art and art-making, and there’s much about that in the book,” Li tells me.
There’s more to come from John Field and Percherette. Two more books, in fact, which will no doubt be full of the same kind of wisdom, although in a different key, to a slightly different tune.
When I ask Li about how her process has changed from writing her first book to this latest one, she doesn’t hesitate to respond.
“You always think, ‘Here’s a story; it has to be told in the perfect way.’ You realize, ‘No. You’re not looking for the perfect way. You’re just looking for one way that you can do it well,’ and that is a good knowledge to have.”
